clue.text: Thus to impede Bunter opening it would be cruel

definitions.text: Thus to impede Bunter opening it would be cruel

parts.words: Thus to impede Bunter opening it would be cruel
parts.note: the word for impeding is also the wicker food basket the greedy schoolboy Billy Bunter longs to open, so blocking him is a play on the same word

explanation.surface: A cruel trick: stopping a greedy schoolboy from getting at his treat.
explanation.walkthrough: Billy Bunter is the greedy schoolboy of British comic stories, always after a tuck basket of food from home; the verb meaning impede is spelt the same as that basket.
explanation.definitionFit: To obstruct someone is to hinder them, and a wicker picnic basket shares the spelling.

clue.text: Paraded — in a cupboard ?

explanation.surface: Something shown off in public, or tucked away in a closet.
explanation.walkthrough: Aired means displayed or made public; an airing cupboard is a warm British cupboard round the hot-water tank where laundry is dried.
explanation.definitionFit: Opinions shown openly have been ventilated; and linen is dried and warmed in a heated airing cupboard.

clue.text: Pride came before it for Jane

definitions.text: Pride came before it for Jane

parts.words: Pride came before it for Jane
parts.note: Jane Austen's novel title begins with 'Pride and', so the word following it in her title is wanted

explanation.surface: The proverb that pride goes before a fall, applied to a woman called Jane.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes 'pride comes before a fall', but Jane is Jane Austen, whose novel title puts 'Pride' first.
explanation.definitionFit: Austen's famous novel pairs pride with bias formed beforehand.

clue.text: Land is so impersonal!

parts.note: in law, property is either personal (movables) or real (land and buildings), so land is the kind of property that is not personal

explanation.surface: A complaint that the countryside feels cold and anonymous.
explanation.walkthrough: English law divides property into personalty (movable goods) and the other kind, real estate; 'impersonal' means not personalty.
explanation.definitionFit: Real estate, meaning land and buildings, contrasts legally with personal property.

clue.text: Premature, like Macduff's birth

explanation.surface: An early arrival, just like the Shakespearean thane's famous delivery.
explanation.walkthrough: In Macbeth, Macduff was 'from his mother's womb untimely ripp'd', born by caesarean, so no man 'of woman born' could harm Macbeth except him.
explanation.definitionFit: Premature means happening too soon, and Shakespeare uses exactly this word for Macduff's early, surgical delivery.

clue.text: Distressed by the thunder, we are out of sorts

indicators.note: distressed means agitated and shaken up, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: letters to be rearranged
letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: People frightened by a storm say they feel unwell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Distressed by' signals an anagram of THETHUNDERWEARE; neatly, the surface is weather-related too.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling slightly unwell or low is an everyday idiom for being off-colour.

clue.text: Like one fated, unfortunately, to hit the wrong note

definitions.text: Like one fated, unfortunately, to hit the wrong note

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters before it are jumbled

parts.note: letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone doomed always to sing or play off-key.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' signals an anagram of ONEFATED; the whole clue describes someone who cannot hear pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: A person unable to distinguish musical pitch will keep singing off-key.

clue.text: She gives me the jade back

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: back means the word for jade is written backwards

parts.note: a jade is a worn-out horse, a nag

explanation.surface: A woman returns a precious green stone to me.
explanation.walkthrough: 'jade' looks like the gemstone but is an old word for a worn-out horse, NAG, turned to GAN by 'back'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Welsh girl's name, so any woman of that name can be called she.

clue.text: Means of rescuing fifty-one cats

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
I is the Roman numeral for one
felines are members of the cat family

explanation.surface: Fifty-one cats needing to be rescued, perhaps from trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fifty-one' reads as a number of cats but gives L and I, Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: Ropes thrown to people in the water are used to save them, and by extension any rescue.

clue.text: Rope-end far from this judicial outcome

indicators.note: the answer is made from these letters, worked out of the words before it

parts.note: the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A condemned man spared the noose by an official act of clemency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' tells you the answer is formed out of ROPEENDFAR rearranged; the surface also works, since a royal pardon keeps the hangman's rope far away.
explanation.definitionFit: A full pardon granted by the Crown wipes out a conviction, a legal result of a case.

clue.text: Blow it ! The beans are spilt !

definitions.text: Blow it ! The beans are spilt !

parts.words: Blow it ! The beans are spilt !
parts.note: the idiom 'blow the ...' means reveal a secret, so 'it' stands for the word that completes that phrase, just as spilling the beans means telling all

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry when somebody has let a secret slip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow it!' reads as a mild curse, but here it is the phrase 'blow the gaff', British slang for giving away a secret.
explanation.definitionFit: In the slang idiom about revealing secrets, this word is the thing blown when a plot is exposed.

clue.text: Just an average worker though specially qualified

definitions.text: Just an average worker though specially qualified

parts.words: Just an average worker though specially qualified
parts.note: 'average' is a marine-insurance term for loss at sea, and the expert who settles such claims is a skilled professional despite the modest-sounding title

explanation.surface: A humble, ordinary employee who nevertheless holds expert credentials.
explanation.walkthrough: An 'average adjuster' is a specialist who apportions losses in marine insurance; 'average' there means a partial loss, not 'ordinary'. The held text's stray '0' is an OCR fault.
explanation.definitionFit: A loss assessor in insurance settles claims, and the marine kind is titled after 'average', meaning shared loss.

clue.text: Hold the baby in Bradford and Leeds

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters of the place names that follow

explanation.surface: Someone cradling an infant in two Yorkshire cities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points into bradforD AND LEeds, where the answer spans the words.
explanation.definitionFit: To bounce a small child gently on the knee is to hold and play with it.

clue.text: Island backs one political party

indicators.note: backs means the pieces that follow are written in reverse order

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I
Lab is short for the UK Labour Party

explanation.surface: An island nation supports a single party in politics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backs' looks like 'supports' but turns I + LAB round.
explanation.definitionFit: An Indonesian island east of Java, a famous holiday destination.

clue.text: An unruly type

parts.note: unruly read as 'without rule' describes someone who rejects all government

explanation.walkthrough: 'unruly' suggests merely badly behaved, but read literally it means against all rule, a believer in no government.
explanation.definitionFit: A believer that the state should be abolished rejects rulers entirely.

clue.text: Dolichocephalically precipitous ?

explanation.surface: A medical term for a skull shape paired with a word for steep and rash.
explanation.walkthrough: Dolichocephalic means having a long skull, so the first part reads 'head, long'; the phrase also means rushing rashly or falling head first.
explanation.definitionFit: Dolichocephalic people are long-skulled; and plunging recklessly or steeply is going at breakneck speed.

clue.text: Ornamental material assessed for rent

parts.note: lace is a decorative openwork fabric
rated means valued or assessed

explanation.surface: A decorative fabric valued for the purpose of letting a property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' looks like payment to a landlord but is the past tense of rend, torn.
explanation.definitionFit: Rent as an adjective means torn apart, as is badly cut flesh.

clue.text: One of seven sleepers

parts.note: the legend of the Seven Sleepers tells of young Christians walled in a cave in a city of Asia Minor who slept for centuries

explanation.walkthrough: The Seven Sleepers of legend were walled in a cave near Ephesus and woke two centuries later; 'sleepers' might suggest railway sleepers or dwarfs.
explanation.definitionFit: The legendary seven youths were natives of Ephesus, the ancient Ionian city.

clue.text: Pray — be seated

parts.note: 'pray' is an old polite 'please', but it also hints at church, where the bench you sit on is in the nave

explanation.surface: A polite invitation to sit down.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is a jocular British invitation to sit down, using the church bench; 'Pray' suggests worship but is the courteous 'please'.
explanation.definitionFit: Colloquially inviting someone to sit down refers to the long wooden benches of a church.

clue.text: The misleading thing about Haddock

parts.note: A. P. Herbert's humorous 'Misleading ...' series of mock law reports feature the litigant Albert Haddock, so each story is one such legal matter

explanation.surface: Something deceptive about a common fish.
explanation.walkthrough: Haddock looks like the fish, but is Albert Haddock, hero of A. P. Herbert's 'Misleading Cases', comic invented law reports in Punch.
explanation.definitionFit: Each of Herbert's mock law reports is a lawsuit, and those books are titled Misleading ones.

clue.text: The Spanish stay up if the food is

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the pieces are read from bottom to top, reversed

parts.note: el is Spanish for 'the'
to bide is to stay or wait

explanation.surface: Spanish diners stay up late provided the food is good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses EL + BIDE to give the answer; the definition completes the sentence 'the food is ...', describing food fit to eat.
explanation.definitionFit: Fit to be eaten describes what food must be.

clue.text: The butter's pretty thin-what a predicament !

explanation.surface: A complaint about a meanly buttered slice of bread.
explanation.walkthrough: The British say butter 'spread' thinly is just a smear on bread; the same word means an awkward fix.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin smear of butter on toast, and an awkward situation one has got into.

clue.text: Sacred river has a beginning

parts.note: Alph is the sacred river in Coleridge's Kubla Khan

explanation.surface: A holy river has its source somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Where Alph, the sacred river, ran' is from Coleridge's Kubla Khan; 'has' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The first Greek letter stands for the start of anything, as in alpha and omega.

clue.text: "An agate-stone On the forefinger of an" (R. & J.)

definitions.text: "An agate-stone On the forefinger of an" (R. & J.)

parts.words: "An agate-stone On the forefinger of an" (R. & J.)
parts.note: Mercutio's Queen Mab speech in Romeo and Juliet says she is no bigger than the ring stone on a civic dignitary's finger; the missing last word of the quotation is wanted

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank line from Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet.
explanation.walkthrough: Mercutio describes Queen Mab as 'In shape no bigger than an agate-stone / On the fore-finger of an alderman'. An alderman was a senior town councillor in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: The quotation completes with a senior member of a borough council, whose seal ring held the agate.

clue.text: Saul's cousin making his point in the bar perhaps

indicators.note: in means the compass point is placed inside the other piece
perhaps suggests the letters of bar may be arranged otherwise

parts.note: taken as written: a bar
NE, north-east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A biblical figure arguing his case in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges BAR as ABR, and 'in' puts NE inside it. In the Bible, Abner, Saul's army commander, was son of Ner, Saul's uncle.
explanation.definitionFit: Abner son of Ner was King Saul's first cousin and general in the Book of Samuel.

clue.text: Fifty to one odds in a manner of speaking

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty
I is the Roman numeral for one
SP, starting price, is the betting odds when a race begins

explanation.surface: A bookmaker's long-shot odds of fifty to one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fifty to one' reads as a betting price, but 'to' is a link joining L, I and SP.
explanation.definitionFit: A speech impediment pronouncing s as th is one particular way of talking.

clue.text: One who lives in a tin bath perhaps ?

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters might be arranged some other way

parts.note: the letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone who makes their home in a metal tub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' signals an anagram of INATINBATH; the surface makes a tin bath a home.
explanation.definitionFit: A resident of a place is a person who dwells there.

clue.text: Bob, taking coach, leaves in it at tea-time

parts.note: bob is old British slang for a shilling, abbreviated s
a coach is a sports trainer

explanation.surface: A man named Bob catches a bus and goes home for tea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bob' looks like a name but is a shilling, abbreviated s in pre-decimal British money; 'leaves' are tea leaves, not departing.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea sieve catches the leaves as the brew is poured.

clue.text: Last to suffer

explanation.surface: The final one to be made to suffer.
explanation.definitionFit: To last is to go on persisting; to suffer is to bear or tolerate pain.
